entities.name: Arnobius the Younger
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Arnobius the Younger (fl. 5th century CE, died c. 455 CE) was a Christian writer and theologian active in the Western Roman Empire, primarily known for his polemical works that engaged with the theological controversies of Late Antiquity. Though often confused with Arnobius of Sicca, his predecessor, Arnobius the Younger distinguished himself through his engagement with the burgeoning debates around predestination and grace, particularly his critical stance against the radical Augustinian doctrines. His writings provide valuable insight into the intellectual and religious currents of a period marked by the decline of Roman imperial power and the consolidation of Christian dogma.

His most significant contributions include *Praedestinatus* and *Conflictus Arnobii et Serapionis*. *Praedestinatus*, a three-book treatise, vigorously attacked the concept of absolute predestination, which he attributed to Augustine of Hippo and his followers, while also refuting various heresies. The *Conflictus*, a dialogue between Arnobius and a pagan philosopher named Serapion, showcased his efforts to defend Christian tenets against pagan intellectual challenges, though its authenticity has been debated. These works reveal a theological position often categorized as semi-Pelagian, emphasizing human free will in salvation and rejecting the notion of irresistible grace, a stance prevalent in certain circles of Gaul and North Africa during the 5th century.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Arnobius the Younger was a significant voice in the 5th-century theological debates, particularly shaping the anti-Augustinian stance on predestination and contributing to the semi-Pelagian movement, whose ideas were influential until their condemnation in 529 CE.
